c.tagline: Azerbaijani heart of Iran, home to the world's largest covered bazaar.

taxi.fareNote: Ride-hailing apps Snapp and Tapsi are cheap and widely used but need an Iranian phone number and rial payment. Foreign bank and credit cards do NOT work anywhere in Iran, so bring cash (US dollars or euros) to exchange for rials and carry cash for taxis and shared taxis (savari).

emergency.note: 110 is police, 115 the emergency medical / ambulance service, and 125 is the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets in the crowded Grand Bazaar and agree taxi fares before setting off.

hood_desc: The historic centre around the UNESCO-listed Grand Bazaar of Tabriz - the world's largest covered bazaar - plus the Jameh Mosque and the Blue Mosque; the essential sightseeing base, dense with caravanserais and rug merchants.

An upscale southeastern district built around the historic El Goli (Shah Goli) park and its lake pavilion, with leafy streets, higher-end hotels, and restaurants; calm, scenic, and popular with families.
Tabriz's modern uptown of cafes, restaurants, shopping streets, and cinemas; the liveliest area for dining and going out (Iranian-style, no alcohol), well served by taxis and the metro.
A central, busy junction district near the university and the Blue Mosque, with mid-range hotels, bookshops, and cafes; a convenient, well-connected base close to the main sights.

water.note: Tap water in Tabriz is generally safe to drink, though bottled water is cheap and widely used.

transit.pay: Buses, BRT and the metro use a rechargeable transit smart card tapped on entry; single tickets are limited. Fares are extremely cheap. Shared taxis (savari) running fixed routes are paid in cash per seat, and alcohol-free by law.
transit.hours: The metro and buses run roughly 6am-10pm; there is no overnight service, so late trips rely on taxis or ride-hailing.
transit.note: Tabriz was the first Iranian city outside Tehran to open a metro; Line 1 is running with further lines under construction. Shared taxis remain the most common way to get around.

train: Tabriz Railway Station - domestic services to Tehran, Mashhad and Jolfa, plus a seasonal international line toward Van, Turkey
bus: Tabriz Central Bus Terminal - intercity coaches across Iran and to Turkey and Armenia

airport.name: Tabriz International Airport (TBZ)
rentals: Local rental agencies (no major international brands; foreign cards not accepted)

transit.m: Snapp/Tapsi or agency taxi to the centre (15-20 min)
City bus toward the centre (no direct metro link to the terminal)

tip.r: Not customary; rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated. Note 'taarof' - a host may at first refuse payment out of politeness, so insist gently.

food.name: Kufteh Tabrizi
food.desc: A meatball the size of a grapefruit, packed with lamb, split peas, rice, herbs, walnuts and dried plums, simmered in tomato broth and cut open at the table.

places.name: Shazdeh Restaurant
places.note: Inside the UNESCO-listed bazaar; kufteh Tabrizi and Shahkar kebab are the house dishes.

places.name: Delestan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Traditional decor and a menu built on Tabriz classics including the big meatball.

places.name: Baliq Restaurant
places.note: Ship-shaped local landmark serving koofteh Tabrizi and dizi to a mostly Tabrizi crowd.

food.name: Ab gusht / dizi
food.desc: Lamb, chickpeas and potato slow-cooked in a stone crock; you drink the broth first, then mash the solids into a paste to eat with flatbread.

places.name: Baliq Restaurant
places.note: Dizi served in the traditional stone pot with the mashing tool alongside.

places.name: Delestan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Classic sit-down dizi lunch in a tiled traditional dining room.

places.name: Tabriz Bazaar teahouses and eateries
places.note: Small bazaar kitchens serve dizi at midday, the way locals eat it.

food.name: Tabriz sausage (sojuk / kalbas)
food.desc: Spiced, garlicky cured beef sausage unique to Tabriz, sliced thin, fried with egg and tomato or stuffed into a sandwich roll.

places.name: Tabriz Bazaar food lanes
places.note: Sausage shops in the bazaar sell it by weight; several counters fry sandwiches to order.

places.name: Shazdeh Restaurant
places.note: Handy sit-down option in the bazaar for local charcuterie and Tabrizi cooking.

places.name: Tarbiat Street sandwich shops
places.note: The city's main walking street is lined with counters doing sausage sandwiches.

food.name: Dolma Azerbaijani style
food.desc: Vine leaves, or hollowed peppers and quince, filled with rice, minced lamb, split peas and herbs, then stewed with tomato and lemon.

places.name: Delestan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Regional dolma alongside the other Tabrizi standards.

places.name: Shazdeh Restaurant
places.note: Serves the Azerbaijani-style dolma that Tabriz is known for.

places.name: Baliq Restaurant
places.note: Large local restaurant with a full spread of East Azerbaijan home cooking.

food.name: Chelo kebab with Tabriz butter
food.desc: Grilled lamb or minced koobideh over saffron rice, finished with a knob of the region's prized local butter and a charred tomato.

places.name: Haj Ali Chelo Kebab
places.note: Beloved kebab house whose special local butter over saffron rice is the draw.

places.name: Shazdeh Restaurant
places.note: Shahkar kebab is the signature grill here.

places.name: Baliq Restaurant
places.note: Reliable, busy kebab and rice plates in a distinctive building.

food.name: Qurabiya and Tabriz sweets
food.desc: Crumbly almond-and-cardamom shortbread, plus nougat, rice-flour cookies and boiled sweets. Tabriz is Iran's confectionery capital.

places.name: Tabriz Bazaar sweet sellers
places.note: Whole lanes of the covered bazaar are given over to qurabiya, nougat and nuts.

places.name: Tarbiat Street confectioners
places.note: Long-established sweet shops sell boxed qurabiya to take home.

places.name: Shazdeh Restaurant
places.note: Convenient stop for tea and sweets in the middle of a bazaar wander.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink whisked with water and dried mint, sometimes lightly fizzy. The standard partner to kebab and dizi. Alcohol is banned in Iran.

places.name: Haj Ali Chelo Kebab
places.note: House doogh poured from the jug with every kebab order.

places.name: Baliq Restaurant
places.note: Serves chilled doogh alongside the dizi and meatball plates.

places.name: Tabriz Bazaar teahouses
places.note: Bazaar counters sell bottled and homemade doogh all day.

food.name: Chai with rock sugar
food.desc: Black tea poured from a samovar into slim glasses, drunk through a lump of saffron rock candy or nabat. Endless refills, no alcohol anywhere.

places.name: Tabriz Bazaar teahouses
places.note: Vaulted brick chaikhaneh tucked into the bazaar's caravanserais; the classic setting.

places.name: Delestan Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Traditional room where tea and qalyan follow the meal.

places.name: El Goli park teahouses
places.note: Lakeside pavilions and terraces where Tabrizis drink tea on summer evenings.

landmarks: Tabriz Grand Bazaar
A UNESCO-listed labyrinth of vaulted brick corridors, the world's largest covered bazaar, glittering with carpets, spices and gold along the ancient Silk Road.
Blue Mosque (Masjed-e Kabud)
A 1465 masterpiece dubbed the 'Turquoise of Islam', its surviving cobalt tilework and calligraphy still dazzling despite centuries of earthquakes.
El Goli (Shah Goli) Park
A beloved hillside park surrounding a grand square pool, with a Qajar-era pavilion floating at its centre and promenades circling the water.
Arg of Tabriz (Ark Citadel)
The colossal brick remnant of a 14th-century citadel-mosque, whose towering walls have dominated the city skyline for seven hundred years.
Azerbaijan Museum
Iran's second archaeology museum, home to 3,000-year-old finds, Iron Age skeletons and sculptor Ahad Hosseini's haunting bronze figures.
Constitution House (Khaneh Mashrouteh)
A jewel of a Qajar mansion where Tabriz's revolutionaries plotted Iran's 1906 Constitutional Revolution, now a museum with a famous stained-glass hall.
Maqbarat-o-shoara (Mausoleum of Poets)
A striking modernist monument of interlocking concrete arches honouring over 400 Persian poets and mystics buried here, including beloved Shahriar.
Kandovan Village
A living troglodyte village an hour from Tabriz, where families still inhabit cone-shaped volcanic rock homes reminiscent of Cappadocia.
Amir Nezam House (Qajar Museum)
A refined 19th-century mansion of mirrored porches and orangery courtyards, now showcasing Qajar-era coins, ceramics, and royal artefacts.
Jameh Mosque of Tabriz
The city's ancient Friday mosque beside the Grand Bazaar, its forest of brick columns and stucco mihrab layered with a millennium of history.

intl.to: Van (Turkey) - with a Lake Van ferry transfer, onward to Ankara & Istanbul

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: Tabriz is Iran's rail gateway to Turkey. The weekly Trans-Asia Express runs to Van, where passengers and carriages cross Lake Van by train ferry before continuing to Ankara and Istanbul - a journey of two to three days that has run intermittently, so confirm it is operating before planning around it. Domestically, overnight trains reach Tehran in about 10 hours. Book through a local agent; Raja's site does not take foreign cards.

intl.to: Istanbul & Van (Turkey) - via the Bazargan border
intl.op: Iranian coach operators — tickets at the Tabriz terminal, no online booking

intl.to: Yerevan (Armenia) & Baku (Azerbaijan) - via the Nordooz and Astara borders
intl.op: regional coach operators — tickets at the Tabriz terminal

bus.note: Tabriz is the practical overland exit from Iran toward Turkey and the Caucasus. Istanbul coaches take around 30 hours via Bazargan, and Yerevan roughly 20 via Nordooz. Border crossings are slow and visa rules vary sharply by nationality, so check before you go and carry cash. Domestic VIP coaches reach Tehran in about 8 hours.

ferry.note: Tabriz is inland in north-western Iran. Lake Urmia to the west has largely dried up and carries no passenger service, and the Caspian ports are several hours east, so there are no ferries here. The one boat crossing you may encounter is the Lake Van train ferry inside Turkey, which forms part of the Trans-Asia Express journey.

half.name: Marand
half.blurb: Agricultural town northwest of Tabriz known for its orchards and centuries-old mosques.

full.name: St. Stepanos Monastery
full.blurb: Armenian stone monastery near the Aras river close to the border with Azerbaijan.

full.name: Lake Urmia
full.blurb: Vast salt lake with pink-tinged shallows, once among the largest saltwater lakes in the region.
